name: Introduction to Psychology
description: An exploration of human behavior and mental processes — from neurons and perception to personality, social influence, and therapy — covering the major perspectives and key findings of modern psychology.

modules.title: What Is Psychology?
modules.objectives: Define psychology; identify major theoretical perspectives; understand the history from Wundt to modern approaches; recognize psychology as a science.
modules.readingNote: Assigned reading for Module 1: What Is Psychology?.
modules.videoNote: GIIS lesson video for Module 1: What Is Psychology?.
modules.video2Note: Crash Course Psychology #1 — Intro to Psychology
modules.practiceNote: GIIS Learn Portal — use the module lesson, assigned course materials, and teacher-reviewed practice inside the GIIS course path; no external practice platform is required.
modules.assignment: Choose two psychological perspectives (e.g., behavioral and cognitive). Write a short paragraph explaining how each would interpret the same behavior — for example, why a student procrastinates. Compare the explanations. Submit: a document, worksheet, slide, image, or link that shows the completed work. Include: examples, evidence, observations, concepts, or analysis from the What Is Psychology? module, plus a short explanation of how your work supports your answer. Evaluation: the teacher should be able to see the final product, the steps or evidence used, and one clear connection to the module objective.

modules.title: Research Methods in Psychology
modules.objectives: Distinguish experimental, correlational, and descriptive research; identify variables; understand ethics in psychological research. Students will interpret sources or examples, explain cause-and-effect relationships, and support claims with evidence in the module assignment.
modules.readingNote: Assigned reading for Module 2: Research Methods in Psychology.
modules.videoNote: GIIS lesson video for Module 2: Research Methods in Psychology.
modules.practiceNote: GIIS Learn Portal — use the module lesson, assigned course materials, and teacher-reviewed practice inside the GIIS course path; no external practice platform is required.
modules.assignment: Design a simple experiment to test the hypothesis that background music affects memory recall. Identify the independent variable, dependent variable, control group, and one potential confound. Explain how you would obtain informed consent. Submit: a document, worksheet, slide, image, or link that shows the completed work. Include: examples, evidence, observations, concepts, or analysis from the Research Methods in Psychology module, plus a short explanation of how your work supports your answer. Evaluation: the teacher should be able to see the final product, the steps or evidence used, and one clear connection to the module objective.

modules.title: Biological Bases of Behavior
modules.objectives: Describe neuron structure and function; identify key neurotransmitters and their effects; locate major brain structures and their roles.
modules.readingNote: Assigned reading for Module 3: Biological Bases of Behavior.
modules.videoNote: GIIS lesson video for Module 3: Biological Bases of Behavior.
modules.practiceNote: GIIS Learn Portal — use the module lesson, assigned course materials, and teacher-reviewed practice inside the GIIS course path; no external practice platform is required.
modules.assignment: Choose one neurotransmitter and use the assigned textbook plus one credible health or research source. Submit: a one-page evidence brief. Include: its main signaling role, one carefully worded association with behavior or a condition, one treatment that affects the system, and two citations. Evaluation: accurate distinctions between association and causation, source quality, and no diagnosis or treatment recommendation.

modules.title: Sensation and Perception
modules.objectives: Distinguish sensation from perception; explain absolute and difference thresholds; describe Gestalt principles and depth cues. Students will interpret sources or examples, explain cause-and-effect relationships, and support claims with evidence in the module assignment.
modules.readingNote: Assigned reading for Module 4: Sensation and Perception.
modules.videoNote: GIIS lesson video for Module 4: Sensation and Perception.
modules.practiceNote: GIIS Learn Portal — use the module lesson, assigned course materials, and teacher-reviewed practice inside the GIIS course path; no external practice platform is required.
modules.assignment: Find three optical illusions online. For each, explain which Gestalt principle or perceptual concept (e.g., figure-ground, closure, depth cue) is involved and why our brain is "fooled." Submit: a document, worksheet, slide, image, or link that shows the completed work. Include: examples, evidence, observations, concepts, or analysis from the Sensation and Perception module, plus a short explanation of how your work supports your answer. Evaluation: the teacher should be able to see the final product, the steps or evidence used, and one clear connection to the module objective.

modules.title: States of Consciousness
modules.objectives: Describe sleep stages and their functions; explain theories of dreaming; understand how hypnosis and psychoactive drugs alter consciousness.
modules.readingNote: Assigned reading for Module 5: States of Consciousness.
modules.videoNote: GIIS lesson video for Module 5: States of Consciousness.

modules.assignment: Analyze a provided fictional three-day sleep log rather than tracking your own sleep. Submit: a table and a 250-word interpretation. Include: estimated sleep duration, consistency of sleep and wake times, two patterns connected to sleep stages or circadian rhythms, and one limitation of the dataset. Evaluation: accurate calculations, evidence-bounded interpretation, and no medical diagnosis or personal health disclosure.

modules.title: Learning and Conditioning
modules.objectives: Explain classical and operant conditioning with examples; describe schedules of reinforcement; apply observational learning theory. Students will interpret sources or examples, explain cause-and-effect relationships, and support claims with evidence in the module assignment.
modules.readingNote: Assigned reading for Module 6: Learning and Conditioning.
modules.videoNote: GIIS lesson video for Module 6: Learning and Conditioning.

modules.assignment: Use provided or fictional examples to label one classical-conditioning sequence and one operant-conditioning sequence. Submit: a labeled diagram and a 200-word comparison. Include: US, UR, NS/CS, and CR for the classical example; behavior, consequence, reinforcement or punishment, and positive or negative for the operant example; and evidence showing how behavior changed. Evaluation: complete labels, correct use of positive/negative, evidence-based reasoning, and an accurate comparison. No personal disclosure is required.

modules.title: Memory Systems & Retrieval
modules.objectives: Describe encoding, storage, and retrieval; compare short-term and long-term memory; explain forgetting and memory distortion. Students will interpret sources or examples, explain cause-and-effect relationships, and support claims with evidence in the module assignment.
modules.readingNote: Assigned reading for Module 7: Memory Systems & Retrieval.
modules.videoNote: GIIS lesson video for Module 7: Memory Systems & Retrieval.

Submit: a document, worksheet, slide, image, or link that shows the completed work. modules.title: Thinking and Intelligence
modules.objectives: Describe problem-solving strategies and cognitive biases; compare theories of intelligence; discuss the nature–nurture debate in intelligence. Students will interpret sources or examples, explain cause-and-effect relationships, and support claims with evidence in the module assignment.
modules.readingNote: Assigned reading for Module 8: Thinking and Intelligence.
modules.videoNote: GIIS lesson video for Module 8: Thinking and Intelligence.
modules.practiceNote: GIIS Learn Portal — use the module lesson, assigned course materials, and teacher-reviewed practice inside the GIIS course path; no external practice platform is required.
modules.assignment: Analyze a provided fictional consumer decision. Submit: a 300-word decision audit. Include: two cognitive biases, quoted evidence supporting each label, one debiasing strategy, and an explanation of what evidence would still be needed before judging the decision. questions.question: Which psychological perspective would most likely explain aggression in terms of unconscious childhood conflicts?
questions.explanation: The psychoanalytic perspective, founded by Freud, emphasizes unconscious drives and early childhood experiences as drivers of behavior.

questions.question: A researcher randomly assigns participants to treatment or control groups. This primarily controls for:
questions.explanation: Random assignment ensures that any pre-existing differences between participants are distributed equally across groups.

questions.question: Damage to the hippocampus would most directly impair:
questions.explanation: The hippocampus is critical for consolidating new declarative (explicit) memories into long-term storage.

questions.question: The Gestalt principle describing the tendency to group nearby objects is called:
questions.explanation: Proximity groups elements that are close together, while similarity groups elements that share features.

questions.question: Research suggests that __________ sleep plays an important role in consolidating emotional memories and procedural skills.
questions.explanation: REM sleep is associated with the consolidation of emotional memories and procedural learning.

questions.question: A child is rewarded with candy every 5 math problems completed. This is a:
questions.explanation: A fixed-ratio schedule delivers reinforcement after a set number of responses (every 5 problems).

questions.question: The part of a neuron that carries signals AWAY from the cell body is the:
questions.explanation: The correct answer is: Axon.

questions.question: By definition, an absolute threshold is the minimum stimulus intensity detected what percentage of the time?
questions.explanation: An absolute threshold is conventionally defined as the intensity detected on 50% of trials, not every trial.

questions.question: When a previously conditioned response disappears because the CS is repeatedly presented without the UCS, this is called:
questions.explanation: Extinction occurs when the conditioned stimulus no longer reliably predicts the unconditioned stimulus, and the conditioned response fades.

questions.question: The "fight-or-flight" stress response is controlled primarily by the:
questions.explanation: The sympathetic division of the autonomic nervous system triggers the fight-or-flight response.

questions.question: Which research method is best suited to establishing a cause-and-effect relationship?
questions.explanation: Only a controlled experiment — with manipulation of an independent variable and random assignment — can establish causation.

questions.question: In the classic estimate by George Miller, short-term memory capacity was approximately:
questions.explanation: Miller’s classic estimate was about 7 ± 2 chunks; later research often finds lower capacity under more controlled conditions.

questions.question: Elizabeth Loftus's misinformation effect research demonstrated that:
options: Memory is a perfect recording of events
Only emotional events are reliably remembered
questions.explanation: Loftus showed that leading questions and post-event information can create false memories or distort existing ones.

questions.question: Which schedule of reinforcement produces the highest and most consistent rate of responding?
questions.explanation: The correct answer is: Variable-ratio.

questions.question: Which perspective emphasizes the role of conscious thought processes in shaping behavior?
questions.explanation: The cognitive perspective focuses on mental processes such as thinking, reasoning, and problem-solving as the primary influences on behavior.

questions.question: On a final exam, psychology is best defined as:
options: The study of the brain's physical structure
The scientific study of behavior and mental processes
questions.answer: The scientific study of behavior and mental processes
questions.explanation: The correct answer is: The scientific study of behavior and mental processes.

questions.question: In a controlled experiment, participants who do NOT receive the treatment belong to the:
questions.explanation: The control group does not receive the independent variable, providing a baseline against which to compare the experimental group.

questions.question: Which neurotransmitter deficit is most associated with Parkinson's disease?
questions.explanation: Parkinson's disease results from the degeneration of dopamine-producing neurons in the substantia nigra.

questions.question: The smallest detectable change in stimulus intensity is the:
questions.explanation: The JND (or difference threshold) is the minimum change in stimulation that can be detected 50% of the time.

questions.question: Which substance is classified as a stimulant?
questions.explanation: Caffeine is a central nervous system stimulant; the other listed drug classes affect consciousness through different mechanisms.

questions.question: A dog no longer salivates to a bell after the bell is repeatedly presented without food. This is:
questions.explanation: The correct answer is: Extinction.

questions.question: Chunking improves short-term memory by:
questions.explanation: Chunking groups individual pieces of information into larger meaningful units, allowing more information to fit within memory limits.

questions.question: The ability to reason abstractly and solve novel problems is called:
questions.explanation: Fluid intelligence refers to the capacity for novel reasoning, independent of acquired knowledge.

questions.question: Which safeguard is required before adults voluntarily join a minimal-risk psychology study?
questions.explanation: Informed consent explains relevant procedures, risks, benefits, and the voluntary right to decline or withdraw.

questions.question: The sympathetic nervous system is most active when a person:
options: Prepares for rapid action during a perceived threat
questions.answer: Prepares for rapid action during a perceived threat
questions.explanation: The sympathetic division mobilizes the body for action; the parasympathetic division supports rest and digestion.

questions.question: Using expectations and prior knowledge to interpret an unclear image is an example of:
questions.explanation: Top-down processing uses prior knowledge and expectations to shape interpretation, while bottom-up processing begins with incoming sensory features.

questions.question: Which change most directly disrupts a person’s circadian sleep–wake rhythm?
options: Rapid travel across several time zones
questions.answer: Rapid travel across several time zones
questions.explanation: A rapid shift in light–dark timing can misalign internal circadian rhythms with the local schedule.

questions.question: Removing an unpleasant alarm sound after a seat belt is fastened is an example of:
questions.explanation: Removing an aversive stimulus after the behavior increases the likelihood of fastening the seat belt.

questions.question: A student learns a lab procedure by watching a teacher model each step and then reproducing it. This is:
questions.explanation: Observational learning occurs when behavior is acquired by attending to and reproducing a model’s actions.

questions.question: A witness’s later memory changes after reading a misleading description of an event. This illustrates:
questions.explanation: Post-event information can alter later memory reports, showing that memory is reconstructive.

questions.question: Which strategy most directly reduces confirmation bias during a decision?
options: State what evidence would disconfirm the preferred conclusion and look for it
Rely on the first number seen
questions.answer: State what evidence would disconfirm the preferred conclusion and look for it
questions.explanation: Actively seeking disconfirming evidence tests a belief instead of filtering evidence to protect it.

questions.question: Which design feature most strengthens a causal claim in an experiment?
options: Surveying only volunteers who know the hypothesis
questions.explanation: Random assignment helps distribute pre-existing differences across conditions so the manipulated variable is a stronger explanation for outcome differences.

questions.question: Which part of a neuron receives many incoming signals from other neurons?
questions.explanation: Dendrites branch from the cell body and receive many incoming neural signals.

questions.question: Remembering the first and last items of a list better than the middle items is called the:
questions.explanation: The serial position effect combines better recall for early items (primacy) and late items (recency).

questions.question: Compare fluid and crystallized intelligence and give one task that mainly draws on each.
questions.answer: Fluid intelligence supports novel reasoning, such as detecting a new pattern; crystallized intelligence uses learned knowledge, such as defining vocabulary or applying a familiar fact. Other accurate task examples are acceptable.
questions.explanation: A complete response distinguishes solving unfamiliar problems from using accumulated knowledge.

quizQuestions.question: Psychology is best defined as:
options: The study of the brain's physical structure
The scientific study of behavior and mental processes
quizQuestions.answer: The scientific study of behavior and mental processes
quizQuestions.explanation: Psychology is the scientific discipline studying both observable behavior and internal mental processes.

quizQuestions.question: Wilhelm Wundt established the first psychology laboratory in:
quizQuestions.explanation: Wundt opened his lab in Leipzig, Germany in 1879, marking the formal beginning of experimental psychology.

quizQuestions.question: Which perspective focuses most directly on observable behavior and learning from the environment?
quizQuestions.explanation: The behavioral perspective explains behavior through learning processes and observable relations between environments and responses.

quizQuestions.question: Short response: Which psychological perspective most directly explains behavior through reinforcement, punishment, and learned associations?
quizQuestions.answer: Full credit: identifies the behavioral perspective and connects it to conditioning or environmental consequences
quizQuestions.explanation: Behaviorism focuses on observable behavior and learning through conditioning and environmental consequences.

quizQuestions.question: In an experiment, the variable the researcher manipulates is called the:
quizQuestions.explanation: The independent variable is deliberately changed to observe its effect on the dependent variable.

quizQuestions.question: Ice cream sales and drowning rates are positively correlated. The best explanation is:
quizQuestions.explanation: This is a classic example of a confounding variable (hot weather) creating a spurious correlation.

quizQuestions.question: The placebo effect is best controlled by using a:
quizQuestions.explanation: In a double-blind study, neither participants nor experimenters know who received the real treatment, controlling for expectation effects.

quizQuestions.question: In an experiment, the variable deliberately changed by the researcher is the:
quizQuestions.explanation: The independent variable is manipulated so researchers can test whether it changes the measured dependent variable.

quizQuestions.question: The gap between two neurons across which neurotransmitters travel is called the:
quizQuestions.explanation: The synapse is the tiny gap between neurons where chemical communication via neurotransmitters occurs.

quizQuestions.question: Which statement best describes dopamine’s role in reward-related learning?
options: It helps signal reward prediction and motivation
It is the only cause of pleasure
It carries visual information from the retina
quizQuestions.answer: It helps signal reward prediction and motivation
quizQuestions.explanation: Dopamine contributes to reward prediction, motivation, learning, and movement; describing it as the single pleasure chemical is an inaccurate oversimplification.

quizQuestions.question: The brain structure most responsible for regulating breathing and heartbeat is the:
quizQuestions.explanation: The medulla oblongata in the brainstem controls vital autonomic functions like breathing and heart rate.

quizQuestions.question: Short response: Name two broad functions commonly associated with limbic-system structures.
quizQuestions.answer: Full credit: names emotion and memory and recognizes that different limbic structures have different roles
quizQuestions.explanation: The limbic system is a simplified grouping, so a strong response names broad functions without claiming every included structure does the same job.

quizQuestions.question: The minimum intensity needed to detect a stimulus 50% of the time is the:
quizQuestions.explanation: The absolute threshold is the minimum stimulus level detectable half the time under ideal conditions.

quizQuestions.question: The Gestalt principle that we tend to "fill in" incomplete figures is called:
quizQuestions.explanation: Closure describes the tendency to perceive incomplete shapes as complete whole figures.

quizQuestions.question: Gradually adjusting to low light after entering a dark room is called:
quizQuestions.explanation: Dark adaptation is the process by which the eyes increase sensitivity to light in low-light conditions over several minutes.

quizQuestions.question: Which depth cue requires BOTH eyes to work together?
quizQuestions.explanation: Binocular disparity uses the slightly different images from each eye to judge depth — it is a binocular (two-eye) cue.

quizQuestions.question: Which sleep stage is characterized by rapid eye movement and vivid dreaming?
quizQuestions.explanation: REM (rapid eye movement) sleep is when most vivid dreaming occurs and brain activity resembles that of wakefulness.

quizQuestions.question: According to Freud, the actual story and images of a dream represent the:
quizQuestions.explanation: The manifest content is the literal, surface-level storyline of the dream, as opposed to the latent (hidden symbolic) content.

quizQuestions.question: A roughly 24-hour biological cycle that helps regulate sleep and wakefulness is called a:
quizQuestions.explanation: Circadian rhythms are biological cycles of about 24 hours that help coordinate daily patterns such as sleep and wakefulness with environmental cues.

quizQuestions.question: Which statement about sleep is most accurate?
options: The brain is inactive during sleep
Sleep includes recurring stages with different patterns of brain and body activity
Dreaming occurs only in non-REM sleep
Everyone needs exactly eight hours of sleep
quizQuestions.answer: Sleep includes recurring stages with different patterns of brain and body activity
quizQuestions.explanation: Sleep cycles through stages with distinct physiological patterns; sleep needs and dream timing vary.

quizQuestions.question: In Pavlov's experiment, after conditioning the bell became a:
quizQuestions.explanation: Initially neutral, the bell became a conditioned stimulus after repeated pairing with food (the UCS).

quizQuestions.question: Positive reinforcement __________ a behavior; positive punishment __________ it.
quizQuestions.explanation: Positive reinforcement adds a pleasant stimulus to increase behavior; positive punishment adds an unpleasant stimulus to decrease it.

quizQuestions.question: A slot machine pays out on an unpredictable, random schedule. This is a __________ schedule of reinforcement.
quizQuestions.explanation: Variable-ratio schedules deliver reinforcement after an unpredictable number of responses, producing high, steady response rates.

quizQuestions.question: After conditioning in Pavlov’s demonstration, the bell functioned as a:
quizQuestions.explanation: After repeated pairing with food, the previously neutral bell became a conditioned stimulus that could elicit salivation.

quizQuestions.question: Short response: A driver fastens a seat belt to stop an unpleasant alarm and becomes more likely to buckle up promptly. What learning process is illustrated?
quizQuestions.answer: Full credit: identifies negative reinforcement and explains that removing the alarm increases prompt seat-belt use
quizQuestions.explanation: The behavior increases because it removes an aversive stimulus; negative refers to removal, and reinforcement refers to increased behavior.

quizQuestions.question: The three stages of memory processing in correct order are:
quizQuestions.explanation: Information must first be encoded, then stored, and finally retrieved when needed.

quizQuestions.question: In George Miller’s classic estimate, short-term memory held approximately:
quizQuestions.explanation: Miller’s classic estimate was about 7 ± 2 chunks; later research often finds lower capacity under more controlled conditions.

quizQuestions.question: What does the misinformation effect show?
options: Memory records events with perfect accuracy
Later misleading information can alter a person’s memory report
quizQuestions.answer: Later misleading information can alter a person’s memory report
quizQuestions.explanation: The misinformation effect demonstrates that post-event information can distort later recall.

quizQuestions.question: Searching only for information that confirms existing beliefs is called:
quizQuestions.explanation: Confirmation bias leads people to favor information consistent with their existing beliefs while ignoring contradictory evidence.

quizQuestions.question: Howard Gardner's theory of multiple intelligences proposes that:
options: IQ is the most accurate measure of intelligence
Intelligence is a single general ability
quizQuestions.explanation: Gardner proposed at least 8 distinct intelligences (linguistic, logical-mathematical, musical, etc.).

quizQuestions.question: A mental shortcut that usually leads to correct answers but is not guaranteed is called a:
quizQuestions.explanation: Heuristics are cognitive shortcuts that allow for quick decisions with reasonable accuracy, though not guaranteed correctness.

quizQuestions.question: Continuing to use an object only in its usual way when another use would solve a problem illustrates:
quizQuestions.explanation: Functional fixedness limits problem solving by making an object’s customary use hard to see beyond.
